Timeline::nanosecond¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Series Timeline::nanosecond() const

nanosecond() is the sole public spelling.

Read The Fractional Second Exactly¶

nanosecond() returns the fractional portion after the whole second, measured in nanoseconds. Valid values range from 0 through 999'999'999. Unlike the coarser calendar fields, its result dtype is int64, preserving the full nine-digit fraction without narrowing.

This is not an epoch count. 123456789 means “0.123456789 seconds within this timestamp’s current second,” regardless of the date. Shape and element order are preserved, and NaT maps to -1.

Example: Nine Digits Of Subsecond Precision¶

const auto events = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2020-12-31T23:59:59.123456789Z",
    "2021-01-01T00:00:00.987654321Z",
    "2024-02-29T06:07:08.009010011Z",
    "",
});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, events.nanosecond());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[123456789, 987654321, 9010011, -1]

Leading zeroes are numeric place value, not stored display characters. Thus .009010011 appears as the integer 9010011.

Choosing A Precision Extractor¶

  • Use nanosecond() when all nine fractional digits matter.

  • Use microsecond() when downstream data is intentionally microsecond-based.

  • Use millisecond() for millisecond buckets.

The coarser methods discard lower digits by integer truncation; they do not round. Keep the nanosecond value if later work may need the lost precision.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Do not confuse fractional nanoseconds with epoch_nanos().

  • -1 is the absent-field sentinel; valid fractions are never negative.

  • Timezone conversion changes calendar fields but not this fractional-second component, because it preserves the instant.
